title: Lorenzo Ruiz (28 September)
hookLine: a husband and father from Manila who boarded a ship in trouble and died a martyr in Japan

cards: A man in Manila with a wife, children, and a steady job at his parish church. Then, suddenly, an accusation of a crime, and the threat of arrest. He does what frightened people do: he gets on a ship.
It's carrying missionaries, and he doesn't fully know where it's headed. It carries him toward Japan, where the faith he grew up in has been outlawed. He wasn't sailing toward martyrdom.
He was running from trouble. Today, Lorenzo Ruiz.

teach.b: Lorenzo Ruiz was born in Manila to a Chinese father and a Filipina mother, tradition says, and grew up close to the Dominican friars at the church in Binondo.
He had beautiful handwriting, so he worked there as a scribe, copying documents. He married, and he and his wife had children. An ordinary, faithful life.
Then came the accusation. What it was, and whether there was anything to it, the accounts leave unclear. To escape it, he joined a group of Dominican missionaries sailing north.
They landed on Okinawa, were arrested, and were taken to Nagasaki. What happened next is why he's remembered. Lorenzo was not a priest or a friar.
He was a layman who had come by accident.
The authorities pressed him, under torture, to renounce his faith, and offered his life in return.

Words remembered from his trial say he was a Catholic and would gladly die for God, and that if he had many lives, he would offer them all. He did not renounce. He was put to death in Nagasaki with his companions.
Jesus says in the gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Every one therefore that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven."
Lorenzo made that confession far from home, among strangers.

The Church canonized him with his companions, and Filipino Catholics honor him as the first saint of the Philippines: not a missionary hero, but a frightened father who, when it mattered, stood still.

how: Saint Lorenzo Ruiz and his companions are remembered on 28 September; in the Philippines and among Filipino communities abroad the day is kept with Mass, processions and novenas.

practice: Bring to mind the Philippines: crowded churches, families in Manila, and Filipinos working far from home as nurses, sailors and caregivers, by name if you know one.
If you pray, ask Lorenzo Ruiz, a man who also ended up far from home, to pray for them; if you don't, simply send them your good will.

wordCard.voice: Lorenzo Ruiz. A husband, father and scribe from Manila, who fled an accusation, ended up in Japanese hands, and would not deny his faith.
